## Overview

The Kogi, also called Cogui or Kágaba, are an Indigenous people of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in northern Colombia. “Kogi” and “Kágaba” are associated in the source with “jaguar” and with the people’s own designation. The Kogi are described as descendants of the Tairona culture, which flourished before the Spanish conquest and built stone structures, pathways, and gold objects. Their political organization is characterized as a living theocratic chiefdom. Kogi culture is significant in the sources for its religious cosmology, ecological understandings, ritual specialists, agricultural practices, oral language, and continued efforts to preserve a way of life shaped in the mountain highlands. The sources also describe tensions surrounding representations of the Kogi as “noble eco-savages.”

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Wool and cotton cloth** — Women pick, card, and spin wool and cotton, while men weave these materials into cloth.

**Traditional bags** — Kogi men and women carry traditional bags across their shoulders. Women alone are allowed to weave them, and bags carried by mamos contain sacred traditional objects.

### Clothing & dress

Kogi men’s clothing consists of a tunic and simple pants tied with a string at the waist. Women wear a single length of cloth wrapped around the body as a dress. The sources state that women pick, card, and spin wool and cotton, while men weave the cloth. Kogi men and women wear only pure white clothing. White represents the Great Mother and the purity of nature.

### Architecture

The Kogi live in villages called *Kuibolos*. These villages contain circular huts made of stone, mud, and palm leaves. Men live in a separate hut from women and children. Each village has a large hut called a *nuhue*, or “temple,” where men discuss matters and make decisions. Divination and concentration also take place there. Women are not allowed to enter the *nuhue*, because the Kogi believe women are more connected to the Great Mother and therefore do not need to enter the temple. The sources also describe ceremonial houses as replicas of the cosmos, with a circular form divided into quadrants and a line through the middle.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They describe Tairona gold objects, which were hung from trees and around people’s necks. The sources name the *poporo*, a small hollow gourd filled with *lima*, or “lime,” made from heated and crushed shells. Men use a stick to extract the powder, suck it while chewing coca leaves, and rub the mixture onto the gourd, forming a hardened layer whose size reflects maturity and age.

### Jewelry & body adornment

They describe the *poporo* as a personal object received by Kogi men when they come of age. Men continuously chew coca leaves and use the lime powder from the *poporo*. Traditional bags are carried across the shoulder, and bags belonging to mamos contain sacred traditional objects.

## Music & performance

They mention dances as one component of ceremonies connected with the life cycle.

Ritual activity is associated with mamos, who are described as tribal priests responsible for guidance, healing, and leadership. Through deep concentration, symbolic offerings, and divination, mamos seek to support harmony and creativity in the world. Ceremonies bless seeds in Aluna before planting, bless marriages to ensure fertility, and address spirits of the natural world before activities such as harvest and hut building. The sources also mention ritual offerings, funerary procedures, and ceremonial speech.

The sources describe two documentary films involving Kogi mamos and filmmaker Alan Ereira: the 1990 BBC documentary *From the Heart of The World: The Elder Brother’s Warning* and the 2012 film *Aluna*. In these films, the mamos communicate warnings to Younger Brother concerning ecological devastation and the destruction of the natural world.

## Dance & theatre

They state that dances can occur among the ritual affairs celebrating an individual’s life cycle, but give no further description.

## Festivals & rituals

They describe a ritual system organized around the life cycle, agriculture, marriage, relations with spirits, and death.

Mamos participate in ceremonies from birth to death. Mamo training begins in childhood, at least before the age of 5, in isolated high-altitude places containing a few houses or caves. During training, two or three novices, called *kuívi*, or “abstinent ones,” practice abstinence in sexuality, food consumption, sleep, and nightlife. Mamos also bless marriages to ensure fertility and bless seeds in Aluna before they are planted.

Burial customs receive particular emphasis. Death is understood not as a tragic event but as a “fulfillment of life.” Burial usually lasts approximately two hours and is performed without prayers and chants. The body is placed in a flexed position inside a carrying net, with a rope tied to the hair. The rope is cut after nine days, allowing the person to be reborn into another world. The corpse rests on the left side with the head pointing east. Offerings are placed at the sides, center, and top of the burial pit and are described as “food for the dead.” For nine days and nights, the soul wanders on a journey that ends in rebirth.

## Foodways

They do describe agricultural production and ritual relationships with food.

The Kogi practice slash-and-burn agriculture, with each family tending farms at different altitudes of the Sierra. These farms produce a variety of crops for family needs. The Kogi also raise cattle on the highlands. Women do most of the planting of vegetables, while farming is a responsibility of the whole family. Sugar and coffee are common crops of trade, and much sugar is made into *panela*, described as a type of Colombian hardened brown sugar.

Food also has ritual significance. During mamo training, abstinence from food is part of the discipline of the *kuívi*. Seeds are blessed in Aluna before planting. In funerary ritual, offerings are verbalized as “food for the dead.” The sources relate this food symbolically to male semen and the fertilization of supernatural beings, describing the offering as a means of multiplying the relevant plant or animal.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Kogi language is primarily oral. Language transmission occurs mainly within families and is important to Kogi cultural identity. In addition to everyday communication, it is used in ritual contexts, in teachings by mamos, and in transmitting traditional ecological knowledge, including agricultural practices and spiritual beliefs. They describe Kogi cosmological teachings concerning Aluna, the Great Mother, the creation of the world, the Sierra Nevada, and the relationship between Elder Brothers and Younger Brothers. The mamos’ warnings to the outside world were communicated through the documentaries *From the Heart of The World - The Elder Brother's Warning* and *Aluna*. The sources state that the Kogi later chose to share their “secret sciences” so that Younger Brother might help change the world for the better.

## Language & religion

Kogi, also called Cogui or Kagaba, is a Chibchan language of Colombia. The Kogui language forms a separate Arwako branch with the Iku and Damana languages. The Kogi language is closely related to Arhuaco and Ika and is primarily oral, although efforts have been made to develop a writing system for education and cultural preservation. Its grammar is mostly verb-final, with subject–object–verb word order. Adjectives follow the nouns they modify, and verbs are inflected for subject and object.

Kogi religion centers on Aluna, described as the thoughts of the Great Mother, the creator figure and force behind nature before the creation of the universe. The Earth is understood as a living being, and humanity as its children. The Kogi honor Gonawindua, also known as Pico Cristóbal Colón, as a holy mountain and “The Heart of the World.” They call themselves the Elder Brothers and describe outside civilization as Younger Brothers. Mamos guide religious life through concentration, offerings, divination, ecological teaching, and ritual action.
